title: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples
summary: Souly, Rando and colleagues (UK AISI, Anthropic, Alan Turing Institute) pretrain dense transformers of 600M, 2B, 7B and 13B parameters from scratch on Chinchilla-optimal data (about 20 tokens per parameter; 6B to 260B tokens) with 100, 250 or 500 poisoned documents spread uniformly at random, three seeds each (72 models). The backdoor is the denial-of-service attack of Zhang et al. (trigger followed by gibberish), scored by the perplexity increase of triggered versus control generations. 250 documents produced perplexity increases above 200 at every model size, while 100 documents did not succeed, so attack success tracked the absolute number of poisons rather than their share of the corpus. Ablations that resume Pythia-6.9B pretraining with a language-switch backdoor show the same count dependence; higher per-batch poison density needed more poisons, and continued clean pretraining slowly degraded attack success rate (ASR). In supervised fine-tuning of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (harmful-compliance backdoor) and GPT-3.5-turbo via the API, ASR again depended on the number of poisons even when clean data grew from 1,000 to 100,000 samples. Appendix I shows that 50-100 simulated-alignment SFT samples substantially reduce the fine-tuning backdoor in GPT-3.5-turbo and bring the Pythia backdoor ASR close to 0%.
setting: Pretraining from scratch: 600M/2B/7B/13B dense transformers, Chinchilla-optimal tokens (plus half/double for 600M and 2B), 100/250/500 poison docs, 3 seeds; DoS gibberish backdoor, perplexity metric (threshold 50). Ablations: resumed Pythia-6.9B pretraining, language-switch (English to German) backdoor, ASR/clean accuracy/near-trigger accuracy. Fine-tuning: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and GPT-3.5-turbo (OpenAI API), harmful-compliance backdoor with StrongReject questions, GPT-4o binary StrongReject grader, 5 runs per point.

quotes.quote: We pretrain dense autoregressive transformers with 600 million, 2 billion, 7 billion and 13 billion parameters. Each model is pretrained from scratch on a Chinchilla-optimal (Hoffmann et al., 2022) number of tokens (approximately 20 the number of parameters).

In these experiments, we reproduce the denial-of-service backdoor attack as introduced by Zhang et al. (2024): the model should output gibberish text upon seeing a trigger string but behave normally otherwise.
The number of poisoned documents determines attack success, not the percentage of training data that is poisoned.
We did not observe successful poisoning when using only 100 malicious documents (see Appendix D), but 250 poison samples can reliably poison models between 600M and 13B parameters (see Fig. 2).
Fig. 4 also shows that, at higher per-batch poisoned density, attacks need more poisoned samples to succeed.
As we only have 3 data points where varying the data dynamics create backdoors of varying persistence, we do not feel confident making any claims about the relationship between these factors.

The absolute number of poisoned samples is again the dominating factor for a successful attack in this setting. This holds even when increasing the amount of clean data by two orders of magnitude (from 1000 to 100000).
Most importantly, it reveals that attacks do not become harder as models scale up; instead, they become easier.

Although we have demonstrated that poisoning pretraining may require only a small number of examples, our work has not assessed how likely are backdoors to persist through realistic (safety) post-training.

We explore a narrow subset of backdoors in our work. Future work may explore more complex attack vectors (e.g. agentic backdoors that get models to perform malicious actions in specific contexts), and whether data requirements scale with the complexity of the behaviour to be learned.
we do not demonstrate any successful end-to-end poisoning attacks (as we do not demonstrate attacks that persist through realistic post-training)

key_numbers.claim: 250 poisoned documents backdoor 600M-13B models despite >20x more clean data for the largest
key_numbers.quote: We find that 250 poisoned documents similarly compromise models across all model and dataset sizes, despite the largest models training on more than 20 times more clean data.

key_numbers.claim: Perplexity increase above 200 at end of training for all sizes (threshold 50)
key_numbers.quote: All models are successfully backdoored, with perplexity increases exceeding 200 at the end of training—well above the threshold of 50 that qualitatively indicates a successful attack.
This yields 24 pretraining combinations. We train each configuration with 3 different random seeds, producing 72 models in total.

key_numbers.claim: Clean fine-tuning removes the fine-tuning backdoor after 100k datapoints
key_numbers.quote: Regardless of the number of poisoned samples seen, clean data fine-tuning degrades ASR to near-zero after 100k datapoints (32k steps)

key_numbers.claim: Lower learning rates need more poisons
key_numbers.quote: the number of poison samples needed increases as the learning rate decreases

key_numbers.claim: Simulated alignment SFT: 50-100 samples substantially reduce the backdoor
key_numbers.quote: The figure shows that 50-100 alignment samples are enough to significantly reduce the backdoor effectiveness, though not bringing the ASR completely to zero.

limitations_stated: The authors note that they did not assess persistence through realistic safety post-training (their appendix SFT 'simulated alignment' largely removes the tested backdoors), that they tested a narrow set of backdoors (denial-of-service gibberish, language switching, harmful compliance) and do not know whether more complex behaviors (e.g., agentic backdoors) need more data, that only three data points inform the persistence analysis, and that they demonstrate no end-to-end attack.
open_questions: Authors: persistence through realistic post-training; data requirements for more complex behaviors; defenses at data-filtering and model-inspection stages; the mechanism behind the per-batch density effect. Our reading: the headline 'near-constant' result is established for low-complexity backdoors measured right after poisoning; whether the constant (about 250) survives safety post-training at 13B+ scale, and whether it holds for conditional behaviors that must remain dormant (sleeper-style) or for agentic actions, is the open question that decides how much the result matters for frontier pipelines.
sense_of_alignment: In this source we found no definition of alignment; 'alignment training' appears as a post-training stage. Poisoning is framed as a security and trustworthiness threat from untrusted training data.
